result: Moving T. gondii parasites exert detectable forces on the surrounding extracellular matrix. Fluorescent microspheres embedded in Matrigel are displaced toward moving parasites from all directions and return to their original positions after the parasite passes.
evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by direct experimental observations shown in Figure 1B and Videos 1-2. The bead displacement assay provides clear visual evidence that parasites generate forces on the matrix, with microspheres moving toward the parasite and then relaxing back, demonstrating the elastic nature of the interaction.

result: Constrictions form at the apical end of moving parasites and remain stationary relative to the matrix as the parasite moves through. All wild-type parasites that move at least one body length form at least one constriction.
evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are well-supported by experimental data from 99 parasites showing 100% constriction formation (C25), with visual documentation in Figure 1C and Video 3 (C23-C24). The sample size is adequate and the observation is consistent across all parasites examined.

result: Parasite motility and matrix deformation in fibrin matrices are comparable to those observed in Matrigel.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by quantitative comparison data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, showing no significant differences in motility parameters between fibrin and Matrigel. Visual confirmation of matrix deformation is provided in Figure 2C and Video 5.

result: The 3D traction force mapping system has a displacement detection threshold of 42-46 nm in 3D (28-31 nm in x-y plane), corresponding to minimal detectable forces of 0.66-0.72 pN in 3D (0.45-0.49 pN in x-y plane). The fibrin matrix behaves as a predominantly elastic material with an elastic modulus of 15.6 pN/µm and viscous modulus of 0.09 pN*s/µm.
evaluation: Claims C28-C34 are supported by rigorous experimental characterization including validation with parasite-free samples (C28), laser trapping measurements (C30-C32), and appropriate calculations converting displacement to force (C33-C34). The methods are well-described and the validation approach is sound.

result: The matrix deforms inward toward the parasite from all directions at discrete, periodic time points, then relaxes back to its initial position. This occurs in all three dimensions simultaneously, with deformation either occurring rapidly (50% of cases) or being held through multiple time points before relaxing.
evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are well-supported by 3D traction force mapping data shown in Figures 4A-D, Videos 6-8, and supplementary figures. The temporal dynamics are quantified (C38-C39) and the 3D nature is demonstrated through multi-axis projections (C37). Background periods show minimal deformation (C40), validating the specificity of the observations.

result: Matrix deformation coincides temporally and spatially with parasite constrictions, with displacement vectors pointing inward toward the constriction. This indicates the constriction results from parasite-generated pulling forces rather than the parasite squeezing through pores.
evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are strongly supported by overlaid force maps and parasite images (Figure 4C-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3). The directionality of force vectors (inward rather than outward) provides compelling evidence for the pulling mechanism interpretation (C43), though this remains an inference from the data.

result: Parasites take 1.6-56.2 seconds (average 6.8±5.2 s) to move through a constriction, with variable timing between successive constrictions. In 46% of cases constrictions occur back-to-back, and in 14% a second constriction begins before the first finishes. Parasite speed increases once the constriction passes the midpoint.
evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by quantitative analysis of 99 parasites and 188 constrictions (C44), with detailed temporal analysis shown in Figure 5A-B and Video 9 (C45-C46). The speed analysis (C47) is based on 20 parasites and 24 constrictions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

result: All parasites moving at least one body length undergo constrictions, and trajectory length is directly proportional to the number of constrictions. This suggests constriction-associated forces play an important role in forward movement.
evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by data from 99 parasites shown in Figure 5C. The 100% correlation (C48) and linear relationship (C49) provide strong evidence, though the causal interpretation (C50) remains inferential. The proportionality strongly suggests but does not definitively prove the mechanistic role.

result: Parasite width decreases from 2.6±0.4 µm to 1.4±0.2 µm at constrictions, forcing the nucleus (normal diameter 2.0±0.3 µm) to deform. The nucleus becomes elongated (width/length ratio changes from 0.93±0.08 to 0.50±0.06) as it passes through constrictions, then regains its round shape.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by quantitative measurements from 15 parasites/19 constrictions (C51) and 9 parasites/21 constrictions (C55), with visual documentation in Figure 5D-E. The measurements are precise with appropriate error estimates, and the nuclear deformation is clearly demonstrated.

result: Fluorescent anti-TgSAG1 antibody is swept from anterior to posterior at constrictions and shed as a helical trail behind moving parasites. All moving parasites examined (n=9) deposited such trails.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by experimental observations in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10. The sample size (n=9) is modest but the 100% consistency (C58) and clear visual evidence support the claims. This phenomenon parallels antibody shedding during invasion.

result: TgMyoA knockout parasites show severely reduced motility (2% vs 36% moving >1 body length) and altered movement patterns (tightly twisting arcs, stair-like patterns) without forming constrictions. These parasites produce no detectable matrix displacement above background, suggesting forces below the detection limit of 0.66-0.72 pN.
evaluation: Claims C59-C65 are supported by analysis of 769 TgMyoA KO parasites compared to 278 WT parasites (C59-C60), with force mapping of 16 KO parasites (C64). The lack of constrictions (C61) and altered trajectories (C62) are documented in Figure 6A and Video 11. The absence of detectable forces (C63-C64) is clearly shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, though the interpretation that forces are below detection (C65) is inferential.

result: TgMIC2 knockout parasites show a less severe motility defect than TgMyoA KO (12% vs 2% moving >1 body length) but move erratically in tightly twisting arcs. These parasites fail to form constrictions and do not detectably deform the matrix, despite moving at speeds similar to wild-type.
evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are supported by analysis of 297 TgMIC2 KO parasites (C67), with force mapping of 36 and 18 parasites (C69-C70). The movement patterns are documented in Figure 6A and Video 12 (C68). The claim about similar maximum speeds (C71) relies on citation to Gras et al., 2017. The combination of normal speed but no detectable forces is puzzling and warrants further investigation.

result: Both TgMyoA and TgMIC2 are required for constriction formation and constriction-associated inward forces, though motility is significantly altered but not eliminated in their absence.
evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by the combined data from both knockout lines showing absence of constrictions and detectable forces in both mutants, while some residual motility persists. This is a reasonable inference from the experimental data, though the mechanistic interpretation requires further validation.

result: TgMIC2 knockout parasite nuclei do not change shape during movement. While trajectory lengths are similar to wild-type (38±9 µm vs 42±8 µm), TgMIC2 KO parasites move only half as far from their starting point, suggesting the circumferential attachment zone converts meandering motility into directed progression.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by nuclear shape analysis (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and trajectory analysis from 1,399 WT and 165 TgMIC2 KO trajectories (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). The interpretation that TgMIC2-mediated attachment provides directionality (C77) is a reasonable inference from the reduced displacement-to-length ratio.

result: The predominant forces exerted by moving parasites are periodic and directed inward toward a fixed circular location in the matrix, generated by the parasite pulling on the matrix. This ring of inward-directed force corresponds to a circumferential attachment zone through which the parasite propels itself forward.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are well-supported by the 3D traction force mapping data throughout the manuscript. However, C80 represents a proposed model/interpretation rather than direct experimental evidence. While the model is consistent with all observations, the claim that forces correspond to an attachment zone is speculative and requires additional validation.

result: TgMIC2-deficient parasites lack both inward-directed forces and membrane constrictions, and their trajectories are less straight than wild-type. This suggests the annular TgMIC2-mediated attachment zone normally constrains directional options during migration.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are directly supported by experimental data from TgMIC2 KO parasites. The interpretation about directional constraint (C83) is a reasonable inference from the trajectory analysis, though it remains a proposed mechanism rather than directly demonstrated causation.

result: TgMIC2 likely plays an analogous role during motility to TgAMA1 during invasion, binding to matrix ligands rather than TgRON2. 3D motility can be described as sequential invasion-like events through circular attachment zones. The constriction during invasion may reflect pulling on the host membrane rather than being squeezed through.
evaluation: Claims C91, C99, and C100 represent interpretive models and speculative hypotheses rather than directly demonstrated results. While these interpretations are consistent with the data and draw interesting parallels between motility and invasion, they lack direct experimental validation. C100 explicitly contradicts prior interpretations and would require additional experiments to confirm.

result: The authors propose modifications to the linear motor model where force is generated by actin translocation at the circular attachment ring. They suggest constriction periodicity could result from periodic actin polymerization or adhesin release, or from stalling of new constrictions against previous ones. The constrictions may be contractile and contribute to forward motion through squeezing.
evaluation: Claims C103-C111 represent proposed mechanisms and speculative interpretations. While C104 (no anterior-posterior bias detected) is supported by data, the mechanistic proposals (C103, C105-C109, C111) and the interpretation of contractility (C109-C110) lack direct experimental validation. These are reasonable hypotheses that require future testing.

result: The authors propose several alternative explanations for residual motility in knockout parasites: forces below detection limits distributed over the surface, compensatory gene expression changes, entirely different motility mechanisms, or context-dependent use of different mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C112, C113, C115, and C116 are explicitly speculative proposals for future investigation. While C114 (TgMIC2 KO shows expression changes) is supported by citation, the other claims represent hypotheses to explain the puzzling observation of motility without detectable forces. These require experimental testing.

result: Background on T. gondii: The parasite infects 30-40% of the world's population, causes typically subclinical infections in immunocompetent individuals but can cause blindness or be life-threatening in immunocompromised individuals. The tachyzoite stage uses unique substrate-dependent motility without cilia/flagella, moving up to 3 µm/s along helical trajectories in 3D matrices.
evaluation: Claims C1-C10 represent well-established background information supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These are not novel findings but provide necessary context for the study.

result: Background on the linear motor model: Motility is driven by the glideosome complex, where TgMyoA translocates actin filaments bound to transmembrane adhesins like TgMIC2. The model predicts continuous anterior-to-posterior forces. Similar proteins in other apicomplexans suggest conservation, though recent observations have raised questions about the model.
evaluation: Claims C11-C19 represent established background on the linear motor model with appropriate citations. C17 and C18 correctly note both supporting evidence and recent questions about the model, providing balanced context for the current study.

result: Parallels between invasion and motility: During invasion, parasites form a moving junction that is anchored to the host cytoskeleton, and the parasite narrows as it passes through. TgAMA1 and TgRON2 are central to junction formation but not motility. Both processes involve rotation around the long axis and may involve helical actin flow. Antibody shedding occurs in both invasion and 3D motility.
evaluation: Claims C86-C92 and C97 represent established knowledge with appropriate citations. C90 is supported by citations and unpublished data. C93-C94 cite prior models. C95-C96 are interpretive inferences. C98 is a novel observation supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10. The parallels drawn are well-supported.

result: Background on actin dynamics: Actin polymerization is nucleated at the apical tip by formin1, and anterior-to-posterior actin flux may occur along the entire parasite periphery.
evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Tosetti et al., 2019; Hueschen et al., 2022; Quadt et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017). These provide necessary background for the discussion.

result: The circular attachment zone may function as a guidance system for efficient movement through various environments. Helical trajectories are efficient for small cells in viscous media. Similar annular constrictions have been observed in Plasmodium ookinetes, suggesting this may be a conserved feature of apicomplexan 3D motility.
evaluation: Claim C117 is speculative interpretation. C118 is well-supported by multiple citations about bacterial motility. C119-C120 are supported by citations to observations in Plasmodium, making a reasonable inference about conservation. The speculation about guidance (C117) is reasonable but untested.
